content.text:
I reviewed both drafts against the tone notes (technical, brief, no generalities) and against how easily a non-specialist reader could follow them.

**Clarity — A.** Letter A uses a dated header, addressee block, and three labeled sections (Performance / What changed in the sleeve / A change to the fee on this sleeve), so a reader can find the fee change without re-reading. It spells out what the comparison index actually is (40/30/20/10), states plainly that the commodity cut leaves the sleeve inside its 4%–12% mandate, and says explicitly that core equity and bond fees are unchanged — the first question most clients ask when they see a fee increase. Letter B delivers the same material in four dense paragraphs with no headings, buries the fee change mid-letter behind "I must also inform you of an adjustment," leaves the index unexplained, never says whether the 5% commodity weight is inside or outside the range, and never bounds the fee change to the one sleeve.

**Tone — A.** These are two engineers who will check every energy and commodity statement. Letter A is declarative and unpadded: "We raised listed infrastructure to 44% of the sleeve from 38%." Letter B adds softening filler that reads as marketing rather than reporting — "Our portfolio construction evolved during this quarter to capture specific market opportunities," "Looking at the broader picture," "For context." The euphemism around the fee ("an adjustment... The fee rate will increase") is the kind of hedge that invites a follow-up call in the wrong spirit; A simply says the fee will rise from 0.60% to 0.75%, gives the mechanical reason, and offers to walk through it. A also closes with an explicit invitation to discuss the positioning or the fee, which B omits entirely — a notable gap in a letter that doubles as contractual notice.

**Overall — A**, and not because it is longer; the added length is structure and scope-limiting detail, not padding.

input.reason: Clarity: A is sectioned under plain headings (Performance / What changed / fee change) with a proper date and addressee block, so the fee change is findable at a glance; it defines the comparison index (40/30/20/10), states that the 5% commodity weight remains inside the 4%-12% policy range, and limits the fee change explicitly to the Real Assets sleeve with core equity and bond fees unchanged. B presents the same content as four dense unheaded paragraphs, buries the fee change mid-letter, leaves the index undefined, does not say whether the commodity weight is within range, and never bounds the increase to one sleeve - the obvious client question. Tone: the clients are a pipeline engineer and a reservoir engineer who want technical, brief statements and no generalities. A is declarative and unpadded ('We raised listed infrastructure to 44% of the sleeve from 38%') and names the fee increase directly. B adds softening filler ('Our portfolio construction evolved during this quarter to capture specific market opportunities,' 'Looking at the broader picture,' 'For context') and hedges the increase as 'an adjustment,' which reads as marketing rather than reporting to this audience. A also closes with an offer to walk through the positioning or the fee; B has no such invitation despite serving as contractual notice. A wins on both dimensions; its extra length is structure and scope-limiting detail rather than padding.
